Benchmark risk of a reliability profile

Source: R/algebra-related.R
benchmark_risk.Rd

Computes \(\sigma_\tau^2 (1 - \bar S)\), the average squared error of the best predictors that are affine in each site's own estimate when the mean and the variances are known.

Usage

benchmark_risk(..., se = NULL, se2 = NULL, sigma_tau)

Arguments

...

Must be empty. The standard errors and the sampling variances are named arguments, because an unnamed vector could hold either.

se

Standard errors of the site estimates, a numeric vector of positive numbers. Give se or se2, not both.

se2

Sampling variances of the site estimates, a numeric vector of positive numbers.

sigma_tau

Standard deviation of the true effects across sites, a number of at least 0.

Value

The benchmark risk, a number of at least 0, in the squared units of the estimates.

Details

For a known common mean and known \(\sigma_\tau^2\) and \(v_j\), the predictor \(\mu + S_j(\hat\tau_j - \mu)\) has the smallest mean squared error among predictors affine in the site's own estimate, and its error averaged over sites is \(\sigma_\tau^2(1 - \bar S)\) (Lee, 2026, Proposition 2(iii)). Under the normal model with independent sites it is the Bayes risk of the posterior means with known hyperparameters. It is a benchmark at known inputs, not the error of a fitted model, whose hyperparameters are estimated. It is 0 at sigma_tau = 0 and approaches the mean of the \(v_j\) as sigma_tau grows.

References

Lee, J. (2026). The geometry of informativeness: A Bregman-centroid diagnostic for partial pooling in multisite trials. Unpublished manuscript.

Examples

benchmark_risk(se = c(0.10, 0.15, 0.20, 0.30), sigma_tau = 0.2)
#> [1] 0.01752308
